title: Indian Student Jailed Four Years in US for $3.7 Million Elder Fraud Scheme
excerpt: Roshan Shah, 22, entered the United States on a visitor visa from Canada to collect cash and gold from elderly victims as part of an India-based impersonation scam, federal prosecutors said.
body:
• Roshan Shah, 22, an Indian citizen studying in Canada, was sentenced to four years in federal prison for conspiracy to commit money laundering
  • Shah collected more than $3.7 million from 15 elderly victims across multiple US states by posing as a federal agent
  • He was ordered to pay $4.2 million in restitution and faces deportation after serving his sentence
  • The case is part of a growing pattern of India-based call center fraud schemes targeting elderly Americans

A Cross-Border Fraud Operation

A 22-year-old Indian national who was attending college in Canada has been sentenced to four years in a United States federal prison for his role in a $3.7 million fraud scheme that targeted elderly Americans, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin announced on July 29.

https://x.com/NewIndianXpress/status/2083365131845874061

Roshan Shah pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering and was ordered to pay $4,228,251.24 in restitution to his victims. According to federal prosecutors, Shah entered the United States on a visitor visa specifically to collect money from fraud victims on behalf of co-conspirators based in India.

The scheme followed a well-documented pattern: co-conspirators in India called elderly victims and falsely claimed their identities had been used to commit crimes. The victims were then instructed to surrender cash or gold to someone posing as a federal agent — a role Shah played — for supposed safekeeping.

Victims Across Multiple States

Court documents show Shah collected more than $3.7 million from 15 victims across the United States, traveling to Wisconsin, Florida, Arizona, and other states to pick up cash and gold before transferring the proceeds to other members of the conspiracy.

"The couple liquidated $526,095.40 from multiple investment accounts and used the money to purchase 1-ounce Canadian Gold Maple Leaf coins."

— Federal court documents, Eastern District of Wisconsin

Among Shah's victims were a New Berlin, Wisconsin couple who told police they had been speaking with a person claiming to be a special agent with the U.S. Department of the Treasury. The couple liquidated more than $526,000 from multiple investment accounts between June and July, using the funds to purchase gold coins. They were told a courier would collect the gold and place it in a safety deposit box in Washington, D.C., for safekeeping.

Shah was arrested on April 4, 2025, while attempting to collect what he believed were fraud proceeds in New Berlin using the same scheme. He told investigators he was a middleman and was paid between $2,000 and $4,000 per pickup.

A Growing Pattern of Cross-Border Elder Fraud

Shah's case is the latest in a series of federal prosecutions involving Indian nationals who entered the United States to serve as couriers in India-based elder fraud rings. In a separate case earlier this year, another Indian national, Dhruv Rajeshbhai Mangukiya, 21, was sentenced to 97 months in federal prison in Austin, Texas, for a similar conspiracy that defrauded elderly victims of hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash and gold.

In yet another case, Kishan Rajeshkumar Patel, 20, from Navsari, Gujarat, received a 63-month sentence for his role in a related scheme that used online phishing methods and government impersonation to defraud at least 25 victims, with total intended losses of at least $2.69 million.

Federal authorities have increasingly targeted these transnational fraud networks, which typically operate through call centers in India that contact American victims, while young couriers — often students on temporary visas — handle the physical collection of funds on U.S. soil. The FBI and Department of Justice have made elder fraud prosecution a stated priority, with U.S. attorneys across multiple districts coordinating investigations into these schemes.

Shah faces deportation proceedings after completing his prison sentence.
nri_angle: The case highlights growing concerns about young Indian students on temporary visas being recruited as couriers for transnational fraud rings, damaging the reputation of the broader Indian student community in North America.
